data.title: Nomadic herders as raiders from the east: waves of invasion in prehistoric Central Europe
data.excerpt: With the author’s permission we bring you Ján Padych’s article about the nomadic herders who came from the east in antiquity and had a hand in the destruction of more than one advanced hillfort in the territory of present-day Slovakia. It follows the waves from the Eneolithic Battle Axe people through the Cimmerians to the Scythians, who stormed the hillfort of Molpír near Trnava.

children.text: With the permission of the author
we bring you his engaging article about the nomads from the east in antiquity, who had a hand in the destruction of more than one advanced hillfort in the territory of present-day Slovakia.

From time to time prehistoric Central Europe became the target of attacks by raiders, nomadic herders who came from the east with the intention of subjugating the peaceful farming population, of plundering, extracting tribute and living at the expense of the vanquished.

The first waves were not as aggressive and predatory as the later ones, yet even so they left a significant mark here. In the Eneolithic, roughly 5,000 years ago, clans of the Battle Axe people came into these lands. They were not, however, numerous enough to subjugate the local population. Even so, something happened at that time, for example in the territory of present-day Moravia, which was undoubtedly connected with their arrival. Firstly, it was an influx of copper tools on a scale unseen until then, and secondly their purely patriarchal social order. Not least, the arrival of these nomads from as far away as Kazakhstan is linked with the beginning of the settlement of the first Indo-European ethnic groups in Central Europe. The local settled farming population came above all from the Balkans, where they had undoubtedly arrived long before from Asia Minor.

A line of large, splendidly fortified hillforts, which may well be called prehistoric towns, ran through the territory of Moravia from south to north in an almost arc-like curve. These hillforts lay about 8 km apart from one another and each of them was engaged in a different range of economic activity. In the “prehistoric town” at Hlinsko near Přerov, for example, a large “manufactory” producing stone tools functioned splendidly. The local stone axes, whetstones, querns and other practical items travelled on carts drawn by cattle to the neighbouring hillforts and from there on to the surrounding settlements and so on. Quantities of woven cloth and fired clay vessels were also produced here. According to a bolder estimate, as many as 2,000 inhabitants lived at one time at this hillfort of roughly one and a half hectares, while the same number may be assumed nearby at the stone quarry. More modest estimates start from the assumption that the nearby settlement merely served the inhabitants of the hillfort during work in the quarry. The inhabitants of these hillforts already lived in a patriarchal order, in which the reins of power in society were held by men. Some finds, however, especially the grave of an old female shaman at an important place inside the site, testify that although female religious cults had considerably weakened in significance and power compared with the preceding prehistoric stages, they nonetheless had their own space and stood in opposition to the more powerful male cults.

These hillforts, and the people tied to them, were experiencing the peak of their expansion and with it a time of plenty. Suddenly, however, a crisis set in. A fair number of copper objects had reached the region and many of the original stone ones began to lose their importance, especially axes, knives and others. The crisis undoubtedly caused the large hillforts to be abandoned out of the blue, and the inhabitants vanished without any archaeologically detectable trace and came back again after some 50 years. Where they were and how they made their living in the meantime is a mystery.

children.text: The only at least partly reasonable explanation would be that they all took up herding, lived in nomadic yurts on carts and moved from place to place as soon as the cattle had grazed off the previous pastures, which with larger herds did not take long. The model taken over from the herding peoples probably did not concern only a change of livelihood and the transition of farmers to the life of nomadic herders. What the leaders of the clans from the hillforts, that is, of the original population, admired in the herders above all was the way in which the leaders of the herding ethnic group had managed to appropriate the originally common property of the clans and how they ruled without limit over the lives of their subordinates. By imitating these models, patriarchal thinking was reinforced among the farming population too, among the inhabitants of the hillforts and settlements, and the original female cults were locally suppressed to the point of illegality, since any egalitarianism was certainly an obstacle to ambitious leaders. New conditions undoubtedly arose in Central Europe at that time, founded both on the inequality of men and women and likewise on the distinguishing of personal importance according to the property owned. In the following periods these inequalities then either deepened or eased.

A further great influx of nomads from the east into Central Europe came at the close of the Bronze Age (7th–8th centuries BC). The tribes of the Cimmerians originally inhabited the steppes north of the Black Sea, from where they undertook devastating raids across extensive territories of Asia Minor, and for a time they controlled a large area there. Their advantage was the use of cavalry to a degree unseen until then, which at first led to their successes. They waged successful wars with Assyria, Urartu and Lydia as well. The turn came after a crushing defeat in Lydia and after the tribes of the nomadic Scythians pressed into their Black Sea steppes in ever greater numbers. Some of the Cimmerians turned to the west and so reached Central Europe. It is indisputable that here too they behaved no more mildly than in Asia Minor, where they carried out devastating raids in an effort to gain the greatest possible booty and sought to subjugate the local population with the aim of extracting the highest possible tribute, and so on. How far they succeeded in this in the territory of present-day Slovakia, Moravia and Bohemia (they evidently did not get any further west) can be judged rather from the legacy they left behind them. In any case, the local farming population of that time cannot be considered meek lambs who would humbly put up with everything. The local Bronze Age cultures venerated the sun as their chief deity. Associated with it was the cult of the warrior, the hero – the demigod. Heroic legends and tales were on the programme of storytelling day after day, evening after evening. Traces of the Cimmerians disappeared in time, yet the legacy of the “lord horseman”, the master over lives, and cruel superiority remained, and they were taken over with considerable willingness by the clan and tribal aristocracy of the local population.

Another of the historically known peoples of nomadic raiders who made their mark in the prehistoric territory of these lands were the Scythians, who, like the Cimmerians before them, ravaged Asia Minor and on their great campaign reached as far as the borders of Egypt, which fended off their raid with an enormous ransom. According to the ancient Greek chronicler Herodotus, one Scythian tribe dwelt in the interior of Europe; they were said to be called the Sikynnae. The name itself partly recalls the old Indo-European term for mounted archers (Skend). Traces of these nomads have indeed been found in the steppes in the territory of present-day Hungary, and not only there. In the period of the 6th–5th centuries BC this Scythian tribe manifested its presence very markedly indeed. At that time two highly militant cultures with considerably developed warrior cults and traditions collided. On the one side the Scythians (the people of the Vekerzug culture) and on the other the people of the Hallstatt culture. Ancient chroniclers wrote about the cruel Scythian rituals connected with war, among the first of them Herodotus. The fighting spirit of young men was to be strengthened by drinking the blood of the first enemy they killed. Every hundredth captive they sacrificed to their “holy sword”, onto which they poured the blood of those sacrificed, whose right arms they cut off and ceremonially threw up into the air and left lying as they had fallen to the ground. Among their most important deities was the sword, a kind of fetish which perhaps did not even have a name (none has survived). It was the counterpart of the Greek god of war Ares, which in itself captures the character of the conquering and plundering ideology of the Scythian raiders, who clashed here with tribes no less warlike.

The Hallstatt culture (named after the town of Hallstatt in Austria), at the time of its expansion, took in a considerable part of Europe from eastern France in the west to the Carpathian Basin in the east, and it also included the northern part of the Balkans. The social conditions of that time are perhaps best captured by the heavily fortified seat at Heuneburg in Germany, where the highest and most formidable walls stood not against an external enemy but against the humbler dwellings in the settlement below. Besides fortified seats and hillforts, there were throughout the territory a number of fortified manorial courts belonging to the clan and tribal aristocracy. From the surviving objects and artistic depictions, especially on metal situlae (vessels), it is evident that the development of social differentiation according to property, and with it importance, had advanced considerably and that the wealthier strata were enjoying golden times. The scenes on the situlae might suggest that Hallstatt society greatly resembled the setting known from the ancient Greek Homeric epics the Iliad and the Odyssey. Feasts, masses of luxury objects, the weaving of cloth, songs, ostentatious funeral processions and so on. From that time there are also known the burials of important chieftains on wagons, after the model of the eastern nomads. A kind of “knightly aristocracy” also came into being, buried with parts of horse harness. (It seems that the later Celtic occupation, which according to the official account led these lands out of prehistory, was, compared with the preceding Hallstatt period, rather a step backwards than real progress.)

The incursions of the raiders from the territory of Hungary led across south-western Slovakia and southern Moravia farther to the north and west. After a stubborn fight they captured the mighty hillfort of Molpír near Trnava, which had stone walls with bastions, unusual for its time, and which had previously appeared impregnable.

Some manorial courts and many hamlets and farmsteads in southern Moravia were plundered. Enormous hillforts such as Kotouč near Štramberk were captured. After stubborn fighting nothing stood in the raiders’ way to the territory of Poland and Germany, from where they returned to their steppes with immense booty. Their incursions also disrupted the long-distance trade on the so-called Amber Road between the southern lands and the coast of the Baltic Sea (a broad belt from the Krkonoše Mountains to the Tatras). At the end of the Scythian rampage the clan and kin aristocracy disappeared from the territory of southern Moravia. From somewhere around that time comes the find from Býčí skála in the Moravian Karst, where almost 40 slain women, men and children were found. The circumstances of the find evidently justify the supposition that it was a sacrifice for the salvation of the land from the incessant devastating raids, and that persons of higher social importance were sacrificed here as “an offering of part of the very best” from society. Subsequently the impoverished land returned from this prehistoric form of “feudalism” to the earlier military democracy. A numerous network of small hillforts came into being, especially on the edges of the uplands; their siting testifies to an effort to face an enemy from the east. The crisis did not concern only the area of Moravia and Slovakia, but affected the whole Hallstatt culture, including the then rich and magnificent west. On the ruins of the Hallstatt culture there subsequently arose the Celtic (La Tène) culture.

There followed still further raids by whole nomadic ethnic groups, such as the Huns and the Avars and others, but this no longer concerned the period of prehistory but historical times, for written records of these wars exist, even by direct participants.

All these raids had one thing in common. The nomads considered themselves superior to the farmers. They went into battle with the ideology of the hunter, as though they were not going to fight equals but to hunt game. They behaved accordingly towards the vanquished and the subjugated. Their practices and their thinking undoubtedly impressed the local magnates of the time as well as their descendants in the distant future. Much later still, in the early days of the Czech state, it happened that for the subjects a foreign enemy used to be less feared than their own superior aristocracy, and that had it not been for the influence of the church, this cruelty would have been incomparably greater. As late as the 10th century AD the Arab-Jewish merchant and traveller Ibn Yaqub reflected on the fact that in the Czech Přemyslid state the lords behaved towards their subjects far more ruthlessly than anywhere else.
